planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring with morning sun and afternoon shade; in zone 9a grow as a large container specimen brought under cover below 30F rather than planted in open ground.

directions: A small evergreen shrub with carmine-red, bell-shaped blooms open just one day but produced almost year-round, this Florida-endangered species has strong wildlife, pollinator, and butterfly-larvae value. The thin, bell-shaped flowers scorch in full all-day exposure, so morning sun with afternoon shade suits it best. Because so few nurseries carry it, start from seed or a cutting from a known Florida source rather than wild-collecting.

planting.note: Plant cuttings or air-layered stock in spring into poorly drained to consistently moist soil; needs winter protection or container culture outside true south Florida conditions.

directions: An evergreen multi-stemmed shrub with velvety heart-shaped leaves and nodding pale-yellow bell flowers year-round, this mallow relative carries strong hummingbird and sulphur-butterfly value and tolerates moderate salt spray and brackish water. This is a swamp-margin species that resents letting its roots dry out, unusual among garden mallows, making it useful for a Gulf-side rain garden or pond edge in warm years. Its nodding, bell-shaped yellow flowers hang downward rather than facing out like most Hibiscus relatives, giving it a distinct look in a native mixed shrub border.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring into open, sandy to seasonally moist soil in full sun; let it self-sow as a low-maintenance filler.

directions: A deep-rooted native wildflower subshrub with a long March-to-November bloom window of orange-yellow flowers, this plant occurs natively across the whole Gulf Coast from Texas to Florida plus up the Atlantic coastal plain, valuable as a low-input, long-blooming pollinator and skipper-host plant. It grows naturally in a wide range of open, sandy to seasonally moist sites — stream banks, pineland pond margins, limestone glades — tolerating both dry sandy soil and periodic wet spells better than most garden mallows.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Sow seed in spring on well-drained but not sandy soil in full sun, mimicking the open coastal flats where it is found; treat any seed source as precious given its restricted wild range.

directions: A rare Texas Gulf Coast endemic known only from a narrow band of coastal south Texas, this woody-rootstocked subshrub carries yellow, dark-red-centered bell flowers and is a genuinely novel addition unrelated to anything else in this collection. It naturally tolerates heavy, often saline clay soils that would waterlog most garden mallows, suggesting it could work in a Gulf Coast saline or brackish garden pocket, though there is essentially no published home-garden track record. This is a little-cultivated species, so treat cultivation details as habitat-derived estimates rather than nursery-tested figures.

planting.note: Sow in spring into sharply drained, limestone or rocky soil; cut back hard occasionally to prevent it becoming woody and sparse at the base.

directions: Native to Texas, Florida, Arizona, New Mexico, and California, this mallow relative carries nectar-rich white-to-yellow flowers followed by distinctive lantern-shaped seed capsules that shatter when dry, and is an important larval host for several skipper butterflies. It naturally roots out of limestone cracks and rocky, well-drained ground, so give it sharp drainage over rich moist soil in cultivation. It flowers in warm weather and holds up to real Gulf Coast heat.

planting.note: Root 6-8 inch stem cuttings with rooting hormone in moist indirect light, then plant into caliche or limestone-based, sharply drained soil in part shade; prone to crown rot in heavier or wetter soil.

directions: Native specifically to the Gulf Coast Prairies and lower Rio Grande Valley of south Texas, this mallow relative carries unusual purple-to-violet flowers from March through August — most relatives in this group are yellow, pink, or red, giving real color-palette novelty. It wants part shade rather than the blazing full sun most mallow relatives prefer, making it useful under high pine or oak canopy in a xeric native bed. Give it caliche or limestone-based, sharply drained soil rather than rich garden loam.
